SupplyNetPy Components.core Module

The Components.core module provides the foundational building blocks for modeling and simulating supply chain networks in SupplyNetPy. It defines key classes representing entities and their interactions within a supply chain.

SupplyNetPy.Components.core

NodeType

Bases: str, Enum

Canonical node types accepted by Node and create_sc_net.

NodeType is a str subclass, so every existing comparison against a literal string (node.node_type == "demand", "supplier" in node.node_type, node.node_type.lower()) continues to work unchanged. Users can pass either a plain string (case-insensitive, via _missing_) or a NodeType member:

scm.Supplier(env=env, ID="S1", name="S1", node_type="supplier")
scm.Supplier(env=env, ID="S1", name="S1", node_type=scm.NodeType.SUPPLIER)

Some types are different names for the same kind of node: "manufacturer" and "factory" both create a manufacturer, and "warehouse", "distributor", "retailer", "store" and "shop" all create an InventoryNode. "supplier" creates a raw-material supplier and "infinite_supplier" an infinite supplier.

create_sc_net looks up which class to create for each type in a table (_NODE_DISPATCH in utilities.py). To add a new node type, add it to this enum and add an entry to that table.

NamedEntity

The NamedEntity class provides a standardized way to display names of the objects in the supply chain model. When printed or displayed, the object will show its name (if defined), otherwise its ID, or the class name as a fallback. This improves the readability and interpretability of simulation outputs by ensuring objects are easily identifiable.

def __str__(self) -> str:

InfoMixin

The InfoMixin class allows objects to easily provide their key details and statistics as dictionaries. This helps in quickly summarizing, logging, or analyzing object data in a structured and consistent way across the simulation.

def get_info(self) -> dict:
    """
    Returns a dictionary containing details of the object.

    Parameters:
        None

    Attributes: 
        None

    Returns:
        dict: dictionary containing details of the object
    """
    if self._info_keys:
        return {key: getattr(self, key, None) for key in self._info_keys}
    return self.__dict__

Statistics 

Statistics(node: object, periodic_update: bool = False, period: float = 1)

Bases: InfoMixin

The Statistics class tracks and summarizes key performance indicators for each node in the supply chain. It monitors essential metrics such as demand, inventory levels, shortages, backorders, costs, revenue, and profit. The class supports both automatic periodic updates and manual updates through the update_stats method, which can be called at any point in the simulation to immediately record changes.

The _info_keys / _stats_keys / _cost_components declarations are class-level, making the tracked set of KPIs declaratively discoverable in one place. Statistics.__init__ copies the _stats_keys and _cost_components lists to the instance before any per-node extension runs (Supplier.__init__ and Manufacturer.__init__ append their own subclass-specific KPIs), so those appends never leak into the class-level list and cross-contaminate other Statistics instances.

Parameters:
  • node (object) –

    The node for which statistics are tracked.

  • periodic_update (bool, default: False ) –

    Whether to update statistics periodically. Default is False.

  • period (float, default: 1 ) –

    Time interval for periodic updates. Default is 1.
Attributes:
  • node (object) –

    The node to which this statistics object belongs.

  • name (str) –

    Name of the statistics object. By default, it is the node's name post-fix " statistics".

  • demand_placed (list) –

    Orders this node placed, as [number of orders, units].

  • fulfillment_received (list) –

    Orders this node received (they arrived), as [number of orders, units].

  • demand_received (list) –

    Orders placed with this node (replenishment orders and customer orders), as [number of orders, units].

  • demand_fulfilled (list) –

    Orders this node fulfilled (sent out in full), as [number of orders, units].

  • shortage (list) –

    How many units this node was missing when orders arrived, as [number of orders, units]. A running total that is never reduced. orders_shortage is kept as an old name for it (§6.6).

  • backorder (list) –

    Orders this node owes right now, as [number of orders, units].

  • disruption_lost_sales (list) –

    Customer orders this site lost because it was disrupted when they arrived, as [number of orders, units]. Kept apart from shortage, which is for units the site did not have.

  • start_time (float) –

    When counting began: the time these statistics were created, or the last reset.

  • elapsed_time (float) –

    Time since start_time. Worked out when read; every average below divides by it.

  • lost_sales (list) –

    Customer units this site never delivered, as [number of orders, units]: the whole order of a customer with no tolerance who found too few units, the rest of an order when the customer takes only what is there, an order too big for the site ever to hold, and what a waiting customer was still owed when their tolerance ran out. Unlike shortage, it counts only units that were never delivered. Customers turned away by a disruption are in disruption_lost_sales instead.

  • waited (list) –

    Orders that had to wait at this site, from customers and from other sites, as [number of orders, units].

  • waiting_time (float) –

    Total time those orders waited, until their units left the inventory.

  • avg_waiting_time (float) –

    Average wait per order fulfilled, with orders served at once counting as 0: waiting_time / demand_fulfilled[0]. Worked out when read.

  • blocked (list) –

    Replenishment orders this site could not place because every supplier it has (or the link to it) was disrupted, as [number of orders, units]. They are not lost: the site orders again when a supplier or a link recovers. A site with no supplier at all records nothing here; that is a mistake in how the network is built, and a warning says so.

  • dropped_qty (float) –

    Units of deliveries that did not fit in the inventory and that no waiting customer could take. The site does not pay for them.

  • inventory_level_time (float) –

    Running sum of inventory level × time (units × time units), up to now. Holding 10 units for 3 time units and then 4 units for 2 gives 38. The holding cost is this sum times the holding cost per unit per time unit.

  • avg_inventory_level (float) –

    Average inventory level over time, each level counted for as long as it lasted: inventory_level_time / elapsed_time (7.6 in the example above). Worked out when read.

  • zero_inventory_time (float) –

    Time the inventory level was 0, up to now.

  • zero_inventory_share (float) –

    Share of time the inventory level was 0: zero_inventory_time / elapsed_time. Worked out when read.

  • disruptions (int) –

    Number of disruptions of this node.

  • disrupted_time (float) –

    Time this node spent disrupted, including a disruption still going on when it is read.

  • availability (float) –

    Share of time this node was not disrupted: 1 - disrupted_time / elapsed_time. Worked out when read.

  • inventory_level (float) –

    The inventory level at the last update.

  • inventory_waste (float) –

    Expired units thrown away so far.

  • inventory_carry_cost (float) –

    Holding cost so far.

  • inventory_spend_cost (float) –

    What this node paid for the units it received.

  • transportation_cost (float) –

    Transportation cost of this node's orders.

  • destroyed_qty (float) –

    Units destroyed in disruptions (see Inventory.destroy).

  • destroyed_value (float) –

    Value of the destroyed units; part of node_cost.

  • node_cost (float) –

    Everything this node spent (the sum of its costs).

  • revenue (float) –

    Sell price times the units this node fulfilled.

  • profit (float) –

    Revenue minus node cost.

  • _info_keys (list) –

    Keys to include in the info dictionary.

  • _stats_keys (list) –

    Keys to include in the statistics dictionary.

  • _live_keys (list) –

    Statistics that describe the present (backorder, inventory_level); reset keeps them.

Methods:

Name Description
reset

Starts the running totals again from zero (for example after a warm-up), keeping the values that describe the present.
update_stats

Updates statistics based on provided values.
update_stats_periodically

Periodically updates statistics during simulation.
disruption_started, disruption_ended

Called by the node when a disruption starts and ends.

Values worked out when read are None when there is nothing to divide by (no time has passed, or no order has been fulfilled yet). The four inventory values are None for an infinite inventory and for a customer demand, which has no inventory.

def __init__(self, node:object, periodic_update:bool=False, period:float=1):
    """
    Initialize the statistics object.

    Parameters:
        node (object): The node for which statistics are tracked.
        periodic_update (bool, optional): Whether to update statistics periodically. Default is False.
        period (float, optional): Time interval for periodic updates. Default is 1.

    Attributes:
        node (object): The node to which this statistics object belongs.
        name (str): Name of the statistics object.
        demand_placed (list): Orders this node placed, as [number of orders, units].
        fulfillment_received (list): Orders this node received (they arrived), as [number of orders, units].
        demand_received (list): Orders placed with this node (replenishment orders and customer orders), as [number of orders, units].
        demand_fulfilled (list): Orders this node fulfilled (sent out in full), as [number of orders, units].
        shortage (list): How many units this node was missing when orders arrived, as [number of orders, units]. A running total that is never reduced. ``orders_shortage`` is kept as an old name for it (§6.6).
        backorder (list): Orders this node owes right now, as [number of orders, units].
        disruption_lost_sales (list): Customer orders this site lost because it was disrupted when they arrived, as [number of orders, units]. Kept apart from ``shortage``, which is for units the site did not have.
        start_time (float): When counting began: the time these statistics were created, or the last ``reset``.
        elapsed_time (float): Time since ``start_time``. Worked out when read; every average below divides by it.
        lost_sales (list): Customer units this site never delivered, as [number of orders, units]: the whole order of a customer with no tolerance who found too few units, the rest of an order when the customer takes only what is there, an order too big for the site ever to hold, and what a waiting customer was still owed when their tolerance ran out. Unlike ``shortage``, it counts only units that were never delivered. Customers turned away by a disruption are in ``disruption_lost_sales`` instead.
        waited (list): Orders that had to wait at this site, from customers and from other sites, as [number of orders, units].
        waiting_time (float): Total time those orders waited, until their units left the inventory.
        avg_waiting_time (float): Average wait per order fulfilled, with orders served at once counting as 0: ``waiting_time / demand_fulfilled[0]``. Worked out when read.
        blocked (list): Replenishment orders this site could not place because every supplier it has (or the link to it) was disrupted, as [number of orders, units]. They are not lost: the site orders again when a supplier or a link recovers. A site with no supplier at all records nothing here; that is a mistake in how the network is built, and a warning says so.
        dropped_qty (float): Units of deliveries that did not fit in the inventory and that no waiting customer could take. The site does not pay for them.
        inventory_level_time (float): Running sum of inventory level × time (units × time units), up to now. Holding 10 units for 3 time units and then 4 units for 2 gives 38. The holding cost is this sum times the holding cost per unit per time unit.
        avg_inventory_level (float): Average inventory level over time, each level counted for as long as it lasted: ``inventory_level_time / elapsed_time`` (7.6 in the example above). Worked out when read.
        zero_inventory_time (float): Time the inventory level was 0, up to now.
        zero_inventory_share (float): Share of time the inventory level was 0: ``zero_inventory_time / elapsed_time``. Worked out when read.
        disruptions (int): Number of disruptions of this node.
        disrupted_time (float): Time this node spent disrupted, including a disruption still going on when it is read.
        availability (float): Share of time this node was not disrupted: ``1 - disrupted_time / elapsed_time``. Worked out when read.
        inventory_level (float): The inventory level at the last update.
        inventory_waste (float): Expired units thrown away so far.
        inventory_carry_cost (float): Holding cost so far.
        inventory_spend_cost (float): What this node paid for the units it received.
        transportation_cost (float): Transportation cost of this node's orders.
        node_cost (float): Everything this node spent (the sum of its costs).
        revenue (float): Sell price times the units this node fulfilled.
        profit (float): Revenue minus node cost.
        _info_keys (list): Keys to include in the info dictionary.
        _stats_keys (list): Keys to include in the statistics dictionary.

    Returns:
        None
    """
    # Clone the class-level declarative lists onto the instance so that
    # per-node extensions (e.g. ``Supplier`` appending "total_material_cost"
    # to its own ``self.stats._stats_keys``) do not leak into the shared
    # class attribute and pollute other Statistics instances.
    self._stats_keys = list(type(self)._stats_keys)
    self._cost_components = list(type(self)._cost_components)
    self.node = node # the node to which this statistics object belongs
    self.name = f"{self.node.ID} statistics"
    self.demand_placed = [0,0] # orders this node placed: [number of orders, units]
    self.fulfillment_received = [0,0] # orders that arrived at this node
    self.demand_received = [0,0] # orders placed with this node
    self.demand_fulfilled = [0,0] # orders this node sent out in full
    # ``shortage`` (was ``orders_shortage`` before §6.6) — renamed to
    # match ``supplychainnet["shortage"]`` so the same vocabulary applies
    # at both the node and network level. ``orders_shortage`` is kept as
    # a read-only alias / accepted ``update_stats`` kwarg for back-compat.
    self.shortage = [0,0] # units missing when orders arrived (running total)
    self.start_time = self.node.env.now # when counting began (moved by reset)
    self.lost_sales = [0,0] # customer units never delivered (other than through a disruption)
    self.disruption_lost_sales = [0,0] # customer orders lost because the site was disrupted when they arrived
    self.backorder = [0,0] # orders this node owes right now
    self.waited = [0,0] # orders that had to wait at this site
    self.waiting_time = 0 # total time those orders waited
    self.blocked = [0,0] # replenishment orders not placed because no supplier could take them
    self.dropped_qty = 0 # delivered units that did not fit in the inventory
    self.disruptions = 0 # number of disruptions of this node
    # Time spent disrupted, kept as the total of disruptions that have
    # ended plus the start of the one going on now (if any), so that
    # ``disrupted_time`` can include the ongoing part when it is read.
    self._disrupted_time = 0
    self._disrupted_since = None
    self.inventory_level = 0 # inventory level at the last update
    self.inventory_waste = 0 # expired units thrown away so far
    self.inventory_carry_cost = 0 # holding cost so far
    self.inventory_spend_cost = 0 # what this node paid for the units it received
    self.transportation_cost = 0 # transportation cost of this node's orders
    # Units destroyed in disruptions (for example, a flood at a
    # warehouse). ``destroyed_qty`` counts the units; ``destroyed_value``
    # is their value, and is part of ``node_cost`` (see _cost_components).
    self.destroyed_qty = 0
    self.destroyed_value = 0
    self.node_cost = 0 # everything this node spent
    self.revenue = 0 # sell price times the units this node fulfilled
    self.profit = 0 # revenue minus node cost

    if(periodic_update):
        self.node.env.process(self.update_stats_periodically(period=period))

elapsed_time property 

elapsed_time

Time since counting began (start_time): the creation of these statistics, or the last reset.

disrupted_time property 

disrupted_time

Time this node spent disrupted, including a disruption still going on now.

availability property 

availability

Share of time this node was not disrupted: 1 - disrupted_time / elapsed_time. None if no time has passed.

avg_waiting_time property 

avg_waiting_time

Average wait per order fulfilled, orders served at once counting as 0. None before any order is fulfilled.

inventory_level_time property 

inventory_level_time

Running sum of inventory level × time, up to now (see the class docstring). None without a finite inventory.

zero_inventory_time property 

zero_inventory_time

reset 

reset()

Start the statistics again from zero, for example after a warm-up.

A warm-up is an opening stretch of a run that is left out of the statistics, because a run starts in an unusual state (nothing in transit, no orders waiting). Run for the warm-up period, call reset() on each node, and carry on running. The simulation itself carries on unchanged; only the counting starts again:

  • Running totals (orders, units, costs, shortage, expired units and so on) are set to zero, including those a Supplier or Manufacturer adds.
  • Values that describe the present (_live_keys) are kept: backorder, what the node owes right now, and inventory_level, which is read again from the inventory.
  • The holding cost is brought up to date first, so that after the reset it covers only the time since the reset.
  • The once-per-time-unit record of the inventory level (inventory.instantaneous_levels) starts again.
  • The inventory itself (inventory level, units in transit, waiting orders) is not touched.

Each event is counted when it happens. So an order placed before the reset and received after it counts as received but not as placed, and units bought before the reset that expire after it count as expired units after it. A partial delivery to a customer takes 1 off the order count of demand_fulfilled when it is sent and adds 1 back when it arrives; if the reset falls in between, that customer order is counted twice in the order count (the units are counted correctly).

def reset(self):
    """
    Start the statistics again from zero, for example after a warm-up.

    A warm-up is an opening stretch of a run that is left out of the
    statistics, because a run starts in an unusual state (nothing in
    transit, no orders waiting). Run for the warm-up period, call
    ``reset()`` on each node, and carry on running. The simulation itself
    carries on unchanged; only the counting starts again:

    - Running totals (orders, units, costs, shortage, expired units and
      so on) are set to zero, including those a ``Supplier`` or
      ``Manufacturer`` adds.
    - Values that describe the present (``_live_keys``) are kept:
      ``backorder``, what the node owes right now, and ``inventory_level``,
      which is read again from the inventory.
    - The holding cost is brought up to date first, so that after the
      reset it covers only the time since the reset.
    - The once-per-time-unit record of the inventory level
      (``inventory.instantaneous_levels``) starts again.
    - The inventory itself (inventory level, units in transit, waiting
      orders) is not touched.

    Each event is counted when it happens. So an order placed before the
    reset and received after it counts as received but not as placed, and
    units bought before the reset that expire after it count as expired
    units after it. A partial delivery to a customer takes 1 off the order
    count of ``demand_fulfilled`` when it is sent and adds 1 back when it
    arrives; if the reset falls in between, that customer order is counted
    twice in the order count (the units are counted correctly).

    Parameters:
        None

    Returns:
        None
    """
    inventory = getattr(self.node, 'inventory', None)
    # An infinite inventory (an infinite supplier) has no holding cost and
    # no inventory level worth recording, as in update_stats.
    finite_inventory = inventory is not None and inventory.level != float('inf')
    if finite_inventory:
        # Charge the holding cost up to now, so that no time before the
        # reset is charged after it.
        inventory.update_carry_cost()
    # Pass 1: zero every statistic listed in _stats_keys (the list of
    # tracked statistics), except the values that describe the present and
    # the values worked out when read (properties such as
    # ``avg_inventory_level``), which follow from the totals.
    for key in self._stats_keys:
        if not hasattr(self, key) or key == "name" or key in self._live_keys:
            continue
        if isinstance(getattr(type(self), key, None), property):
            continue
        current = getattr(self, key)
        if isinstance(current, list):
            setattr(self, key, [0, 0])
        elif isinstance(current, (int, float)):
            setattr(self, key, 0)
    # Pass 2: a safety net for any counter that is not in the tracked list
    # but used to be reset by the old "reset everything" sweep. It looks
    # only at this Statistics object, never at the node's units or orders.
    for key, value in vars(self).items():
        if key.startswith("_") or key in self._stats_keys or key in self._live_keys:
            continue
        if isinstance(value, list):
            setattr(self, key, [0, 0])
        elif isinstance(value, (int, float)):
            setattr(self, key, 0)
    # Some counters live on the Inventory object, not on Statistics, so they
    # have to be reset here by hand. If you add a new Inventory counter that
    # should reset, add it to this block (or move the counter onto
    # Statistics by listing it in _stats_keys).
    if inventory is not None:
        inventory.carry_cost = 0
        inventory.waste = 0
        inventory.level_time = 0
        inventory.zero_level_time = 0
        inventory.instantaneous_levels = []
    if finite_inventory:
        self.inventory_level = inventory.level
    # The clock starts again, so every average covers only the time since
    # the reset. A disruption going on now is counted from now on; it does
    # not add to ``disruptions``, because it started before the reset.
    now = self.node.env.now
    self.start_time = now
    self._disrupted_time = 0
    if self._disrupted_since is not None:
        self._disrupted_since = now

def update_stats(self,**kwargs):
    """
    Update the statistics with the given keyword arguments.

    Parameters:
        **kwargs: keyword arguments containing the statistics to update.
            ``orders_shortage=`` is still accepted as the old name for
            ``shortage=`` (the attribute was renamed).

    Attributes:
        None

    Returns:
        None
    """
    # ``orders_shortage`` was renamed to ``shortage``. Older code (and some
    # examples) still pass the old name, so map it onto the new one here and
    # let both names update the same counter. If a caller passes both, the
    # new name wins.
    if "orders_shortage" in kwargs and "shortage" not in kwargs:
        kwargs["shortage"] = kwargs.pop("orders_shortage")
    elif "orders_shortage" in kwargs:
        kwargs.pop("orders_shortage")
    for key, value in kwargs.items():
        if hasattr(self, key):
            attr = getattr(self, key)
            if isinstance(attr, list): # value = [v1,v2]
                attr[0] += value[0]
                attr[1] += value[1]
                setattr(self, key, attr) # update the attribute with the new value
            else:
                attr += value
                setattr(self, key, attr) # update the attribute with the new value
        else:
            # Most likely a typo in a custom policy or callback. The value is
            # ignored, so the user is warned (the text leaves out the node,
            # so each unknown name is shown once).
            global_logger.warning(f"{self.node.ID}: update_stats got an unknown statistic '{key}'; it is ignored.")
            warnings.warn(f"update_stats got an unknown statistic '{key}', so it is ignored. "
                          f"Check the name for a typo.", UserWarning, stacklevel=2)
    if hasattr(self.node, 'inventory'):
        if self.node.inventory.level != float('inf'):
            self.inventory_level = self.node.inventory.level if hasattr(self.node, 'inventory') else 0
            self.node.inventory.update_carry_cost()
            self.inventory_carry_cost = self.node.inventory.carry_cost
            self.inventory_waste = self.node.inventory.waste if hasattr(self.node.inventory, 'waste') else 0
    self.node_cost = sum(getattr(self, name) for name in self._cost_components)
    self.revenue = self.demand_fulfilled[1] * self.node.sell_price if hasattr(self.node, 'sell_price') else 0
    self.profit = self.revenue - self.node_cost

def update_stats_periodically(self, period):
    """
    Update the statistics periodically.

    Parameters:
        period (float): period for periodic update of statistics

    Attributes:
        None

    Returns:
        generator: a generator that yields after the specified period
    """
    while True:
        yield self.node.env.timeout(period)
        self.update_stats()

LinkStatistics 

LinkStatistics(link)

Bases: InfoMixin

The LinkStatistics class records what flows over one link: the replenishment orders its buyer placed over it, what arrived, how long the orders waited and travelled, what they cost, and the link's own disruptions. Every link has one, as link.stats, created with the link.

Node statistics say how much a site ordered and received in total, but not from whom. A buyer with two suppliers has a link to each, and each link counts only the orders sent over it. A site finds the links it orders over in node.suppliers, and the links its buyers order over in node.buyers. The same events are counted in the node statistics too, so the totals over a buyer's links add up to the buyer's own figures. Customers do not order over links, so customer orders are not in any link (each Demand has its own statistics).

Running totals are kept, not a record of each order. Values worked out when read are properties, and are None when there is nothing to divide by (a fill rate of 0 would look like a very bad link).

Two spreads of order sizes. Both are sample standard deviations (how far values usually are from their average, dividing by one less than the number of values), and both are None with fewer than two values. order_size_std takes one value per order: the size of each order. units_per_time_unit_std takes one value per time unit: the units ordered in that time unit, with time units in which nothing was ordered counting as 0. The two can disagree completely. A distributor that orders 60 units at time 3 and 60 units at time 7, and nothing in between, has an order_size_std of 0 (every order is the same size) but a large units_per_time_unit_std (the orders come in bursts). The bullwhip effect (orders becoming more uneven as they pass from the customers towards the raw-material suppliers) is measured per time unit: compare a link's units_per_time_unit_std with the spread of customer demand per time unit.

Parameters:
  • link (Link) –

    The link whose statistics these are.
Attributes:
  • link (Link) –

    The link whose statistics these are.

  • name (str) –

    Name of the statistics object: the link's ID followed by " statistics".

  • start_time (float) –

    When counting began: the time the link was created, or the last reset.

  • elapsed_time (float) –

    Time since start_time. Worked out when read.

  • demand_placed (list) –

    Replenishment orders the buyer placed over the link, as [number of orders, units].

  • fulfillment_received (list) –

    Orders that arrived at the buyer, as [number of orders, units]. Only the units the buyer accepted are counted, as in the buyer's own statistics.

  • shortage (list) –

    How many units the supplier was missing when this buyer's orders reached it, as [number of orders, units]. A running total that is never reduced.

  • backorder (list) –

    This buyer's orders waiting at the supplier right now, as [number of orders, units].

  • waited (list) –

    Orders that had to wait at the supplier, as [number of orders, units]. Unlike backorder, it is a running total, so it still counts an order once the order is served.

  • blocked (list) –

    Orders the buyer was about to send over this link but could not place, because the link or the supplier's site was disrupted by then, as [number of orders, units]. Orders blocked before any link was chosen (every supplier disrupted) are counted only in the buyer's node statistics. Links from raw-material suppliers never record any.

  • transportation_cost (float) –

    Transportation cost of the orders placed over the link.

  • inventory_spend_cost (float) –

    What the buyer paid for the units it received over the link.

  • waiting_time (float) –

    Total time orders waited at the supplier, from being placed until their units left the supplier's inventory (orders served at once wait 0). Added when the order arrives.

  • lead_time (float) –

    Total lead time of the orders that arrived.

  • avg_waiting_time (float) –

    Average wait per order received: waiting_time / fulfillment_received[0]. Worked out when read.

  • avg_lead_time (float) –

    Average lead time per order received: lead_time / fulfillment_received[0]. Worked out when read.

  • avg_order_cycle_time (float) –

    Average time from placing an order until it arrives: avg_waiting_time + avg_lead_time. Worked out when read.

  • fill_rate (float) –

    Share of the units ordered that the supplier sent at once: 1 - waited[1] / demand_placed[1]. An order that had to wait counts as not sent at once, even if part of it was there. Worked out when read.

  • order_fill_rate (float) –

    The same share counted in orders: 1 - waited[0] / demand_placed[0]. Worked out when read.

  • orders_per_time_unit (float) –

    Orders placed per time unit: demand_placed[0] / elapsed_time. Worked out when read.

  • units_per_time_unit (float) –

    Units ordered per time unit: demand_placed[1] / elapsed_time. Worked out when read.

  • order_size_mean (float) –

    Average size of the orders placed. Worked out when read.

  • order_size_std (float) –

    Standard deviation of the size of the orders placed (see above). Worked out when read.

  • units_per_time_unit_std (float) –

    Standard deviation of the units ordered in each time unit (see above). Time units are counted from start_time and are 1 long. The time unit still going on is left out. Worked out when read.

  • disruptions (int) –

    Number of disruptions of the link.

  • disrupted_time (float) –

    Time the link spent disrupted, including a disruption still going on when it is read. A link set to "inactive" by hand, rather than by its disruption process, is not counted.

  • availability (float) –

    Share of time the link was not disrupted: 1 - disrupted_time / elapsed_time. Worked out when read.

  • _info_keys (list) –

    Keys to include in the info dictionary.

  • _stats_keys (list) –

    Keys to include in the statistics dictionary.

  • _live_keys (list) –

    Statistics that describe the present (backorder); reset keeps them.

def __init__(self, link):
    """
    Initialize the statistics object.

    Parameters:
        link (Link): The link whose statistics these are.

    Returns:
        None
    """
    self.link = link
    self.name = f"{link.ID} statistics"
    self._clear_totals()
    self.backorder = [0, 0] # this buyer's orders waiting at the supplier right now
    self.start_time = link.env.now # when counting began (moved by reset)
    # Time spent disrupted, kept as the total of disruptions that have
    # ended plus the start of the one going on now (if any), so that
    # ``disrupted_time`` can include the ongoing part when it is read.
    self._disrupted_since = None

def record_order(self, quantity):
    """
    Add the size of one order placed over the link to the two spreads of
    order sizes (see the class description). Called together with
    ``update_stats(demand_placed=...)``.

    Parameters:
        quantity (float): Units ordered.

    Returns:
        None
    """
    self._order_sizes = self._add_value(self._order_sizes, quantity)
    now = self._time_unit_now()
    if now > self._current_time_unit:
        # A new time unit has started since the last order: store the
        # finished ones and start counting this one.
        self._per_time_unit = self._per_time_unit_up_to_now()
        self._current_time_unit = now
        self._current_units = 0
    self._current_units += quantity

def update_stats(self, **kwargs):
    """
    Add the given amounts to the running totals, for example
    ``update_stats(demand_placed=[1, 50], transportation_cost=5)``.
    ``[number of orders, units]`` pairs are added pair by pair.

    Parameters:
        **kwargs: The statistics to add to, by name, with the amounts to add.

    Returns:
        None
    """
    for key, value in kwargs.items():
        stored = (key in self._stats_keys and key != "name"
                  and not isinstance(getattr(type(self), key, None), property))
        if not stored:
            # Most likely a typo. The value is ignored, so the user is
            # warned (the text leaves out the link, so each unknown name
            # is shown once).
            global_logger.warning(f"{self.link.ID}: update_stats got an unknown statistic '{key}'; it is ignored.")
            warnings.warn(f"update_stats got an unknown statistic '{key}', so it is ignored. "
                          f"Check the name for a typo.", UserWarning, stacklevel=2)
            continue
        current = getattr(self, key)
        if isinstance(current, list):
            current[0] += value[0]
            current[1] += value[1]
        else:
            setattr(self, key, current + value)

def reset(self):
    """
    Start the statistics again from zero, for example after a warm-up (see
    ``Statistics.reset``). The simulation carries on unchanged; only the
    counting starts again:

    - Running totals and both spreads of order sizes are set to zero.
    - ``backorder`` is kept: orders waiting at the reset are still waiting
      after it.
    - ``start_time`` becomes now, so every average and every value per time
      unit covers only the time since the reset.
    - A disruption going on now is counted from now on. It does not add to
      ``disruptions``, because it started before the reset.

    Each event is counted when it happens. So an order placed before the
    reset and received after it counts as received but not as placed. The
    averages stay correct, because each one divides by a count recorded at
    the same moment as its total.

    Parameters:
        None

    Returns:
        None
    """
    self._clear_totals()
    now = self.link.env.now
    self.start_time = now
    if self._disrupted_since is not None:
        self._disrupted_since = now

RawMaterial 

RawMaterial(ID: str, name: str, extraction_quantity: float, extraction_time: float, mining_cost: float, cost: float)

Bases: NamedEntity, InfoMixin

The RawMaterial class represents a raw material: what a raw-material supplier mines and a manufacturer uses up. A raw-material supplier mines extraction_quantity units every extraction_time time units, at mining_cost per unit, and sells them at cost per unit. (The parameter names say "extraction"; it means the same as mining.)

Parameters:
  • ID (str) –

    ID of the raw material.

  • name (str) –

    Name of the raw material.

  • extraction_quantity (float) –

    Units mined in each round of mining.

Bases: NamedEntity, InfoMixin

The Product class represents the product that a manufacturer makes and other sites buy and sell. It defines the manufacturing cost, the manufacturing time, the sell price, and the raw materials needed to make one unit. A manufacturer makes it in production batches: at most batch_size units at a time, each production batch taking manufacturing_time.

             sell_price: float,
             raw_materials: list,
             batch_size: int,

    """
    Initialize the product object.

    Performs input validation for positive and non-negative values, and ensures raw materials are provided.

    Parameters:
        ID (str): ID of the product (alphanumeric)
        name (str): Name of the product
        manufacturing_cost (float): Manufacturing cost per unit
        manufacturing_time (float): Time units to make one production batch
        sell_price (float): Sell price per unit
        buy_price (float, optional): Buy price per unit (default is 0)
        raw_materials (list): List of (raw material, quantity) tuples: the raw materials needed to make one unit
        batch_size (int): The most units made in one production batch

    Attributes:
        _info_keys (list): List of keys to include in the info dictionary
        _stats_keys (list): List of keys to include in the statistics dictionary
        ID (str): ID of the product
        name (str): Name of the product
        manufacturing_cost (float): Manufacturing cost per unit
        manufacturing_time (float): Time units to make one production batch
        sell_price (float): Sell price per unit
        buy_price (float): Buy price per unit (default is 0)
        raw_materials (list): List of (raw material, quantity) tuples needed to make one unit
        batch_size (int): The most units made in one production batch

    Returns:
        None

    Raises:
        ValueError: If validations fail for positive values, non-negative values, or empty raw materials list.
    """
    validate_positive("Manufacturing cost", manufacturing_cost)
    validate_non_negative("Manufacturing time", manufacturing_time)
    validate_positive("Sell price", sell_price)
    validate_non_negative("Buy price", buy_price)
    validate_positive("Units per cycle", batch_size)
    if raw_materials is None or len(raw_materials) == 0:
        global_logger.error("Raw materials cannot be empty.")
        raise ValueError("Raw materials cannot be empty.")
    for raw_mat in raw_materials:
        if not isinstance(raw_mat[0], RawMaterial):
            raise ValueError("Invalid raw material.")
        if raw_mat[1] <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Invalid quantity for raw material.")

    self.ID = ID # ID of the product (alphanumeric)
    self.name = name # name of the product
    self.manufacturing_cost = manufacturing_cost # manufacturing cost of the product (per unit)
    self.manufacturing_time = manufacturing_time # time units to make one production batch
    self.sell_price = sell_price # sell price per unit
    self.buy_price = buy_price # buy price per unit (default: 0)
    self.raw_materials = raw_materials # (raw material, quantity) tuples needed to make one unit
    self.batch_size = batch_size # the most units made in one production batch

InventoryReplenishment 

InventoryReplenishment(env: Environment, node: object, params: dict)

Bases: InfoMixin, NamedEntity

The InventoryReplenishment class is the base for all replenishment policies in SupplyNetPy: the rules a site follows to decide when to place a replenishment order and how many units to order.

This class is not used directly. Each policy is a subclass, such as the (s, S) policy (SSReplenishment), the (R, Q) policy (RQReplenishment) and the periodic policy (PeriodicReplenishment).

A subclass overrides the run method with its rule. run runs as a SimPy process for the whole simulation. A policy usually checks the node's inventory position each time the node's inventory drops (the inventory_drop event), or at fixed intervals.

How a custom policy should talk to its node. A policy should use these four helper methods instead of reaching into the node's internal attributes:

  • self.node.position() — the inventory position: inventory level plus units in transit, minus units the node still owes (to other sites and to waiting customers).
  • self.node.place_order(quantity) — picks a supplier using the node's supplier-selection policy and places the replenishment order. This replaces calling selection_policy.select(...) and env.process(process_order(...)) yourself.
  • self.node.wait_for_drop() — used as yield from self.node.wait_for_drop() to wait until the inventory drops; on wake-up it safely replaces the inventory_drop event with a fresh one.
  • Link.available_quantity() — lets a supplier-selection policy check a supplier's inventory level without reading link.source.inventory.level directly.

Sticking to these helpers keeps a policy from depending on how a particular node is built, so it works with any future Node type that offers the same methods.

Parameters:
  • env (Environment) –

    Simulation environment.

  • node (object) –

    Node to which this policy applies.

  • params (dict) –

    Parameters for the replenishment policy.

Parameters a policy does not use. Each built-in policy lists the keys it reads from params in _param_keys. Any other key is ignored by the policy, so a warning names it and asks whether another policy was meant (for example, 'T' is read only by the periodic policy). A custom policy can set its own _param_keys to get the same check; if it does not, nothing is checked.

Attributes:
  • _info_keys (list) –

    List of keys to include in the info dictionary.

  • _param_keys (tuple) –

    Keys this policy reads from params, or None if it does not say.

  • env (Environment) –

    Simulation environment.

  • node (object) –

    Node to which this policy applies.

  • params (dict) –

    Parameters for the replenishment policy.

SSReplenishment 

SSReplenishment(env, node, params)

Bases: InventoryReplenishment

Implements the (s, S) replenishment policy, with an optional safety stock.

When the inventory position falls to the reorder point s or below, the node places a replenishment order big enough to bring its inventory position back up to the order-up-to level S. If a safety stock is given, it is added to both s and S. The inventory position is checked each time the node's inventory drops, or every period time units if a period is given, starting after an optional first review delay. The supplier is chosen by the node's supplier-selection policy.

Parameters:
  • env (Environment) –

    Simulation environment.

  • node (object) –

    Node to which this policy applies.

  • params (dict) –

    Replenishment policy parameters (s, S) and optional parameters (safety_stock, first_review_delay, period).

    Replenishment policy parameters.

    Replenishment policy name.

  • first_review_delay (float) –

    Time units to wait before the first check of the inventory position.

  • period (float) –

    Time units between checks. 0 (the default) means checking each time the inventory drops.

def __init__(self, env, node, params):
    """ 
    Initialize the replenishment policy object.

    Parameters:
        env (simpy.Environment): simulation environment
        node (object): node to which this policy applies
        params (dict): parameters for the replenishment policy (s, S)

    Attributes:
        _info_keys (list): list of keys to include in the info dictionary
        env (simpy.Environment): simulation environment
        node (object): node to which this policy applies
        params (dict): parameters for the replenishment policy (s, S)
        name (str): replenishment policy name
        first_review_delay (float): time units to wait before the first check of the inventory position
        period (float): time units between checks; 0 means checking each time the inventory drops

    Returns:
        None
    """
    validate_non_negative("Reorder point (s)", params['s']) # s must not be negative
    validate_positive("Order-up-to level (S)", params['S']) # S must be positive
    if 's' not in params or 'S' not in params:
        raise ValueError("Parameters 's' and 'S' must be provided for the (s, S) replenishment policy.")
    if params['s'] > params['S']:
        raise ValueError("Reorder point (s) must be less than or equal to order-up-to level (S).")
    super().__init__(env, node, params)
    self.name = "min-max replenishment (s, S)"
    self.first_review_delay = params.get('first_review_delay', 0)
    self.period = params.get('period',0)

def run(self):
    """
    Runs the (s, S) policy for the whole simulation: checks the inventory position and places
    replenishment orders.

    Parameters:
        None

    Attributes: 
        s (float): reorder point
        S (float): order-up-to level

    Returns:
        None    
    """
    s, S = self.params['s'], self.params['S']  # get the reorder point and order-up-to level
    # (__init__ has already checked that s is not above S.)

    if 'safety_stock' in self.params: # check if safety_stock is specified
        validate_positive("Safety stock", self.params['safety_stock'])
        self.name = "min-max with safety replenishment (s, S, safety_stock)"
        s += self.params['safety_stock']
        S += self.params['safety_stock']

    if self.first_review_delay > 0: # wait before the first check, if a first review delay is given
        yield self.env.timeout(self.first_review_delay)

    while True: # check for the whole simulation
        self.node.logger.info(f"{self.env.now:.4f}:{self.node.ID}: Inventory levels:{self.node.inventory.level}, on hand:{self.node.inventory.on_hand}")
        position = self.node.position()
        if position <= s:
            self.node.place_order(S - position)

        if self.period == 0: # no period: check again when the inventory drops
            yield from self.node.wait_for_drop()
        elif self.period: # a period is given: check again after it
            yield self.env.timeout(self.period)

RQReplenishment 

RQReplenishment(env, node, params)

Bases: InventoryReplenishment

Implements the (R, Q) replenishment policy.

When the inventory position falls to the reorder point R or below, the node places a replenishment order of a fixed Q units.

The inventory position is checked each time the node's inventory drops if period is 0 (the default), or every period time units if a positive period is given. An optional first review delay sets how long to wait before the first check.

The supplier is chosen by the node's supplier-selection policy. If the supplier cannot fill the order at once, a shortage is recorded at the supplier.

    Simulation environment.

    """
    Runs the (R, Q) policy for the whole simulation: places a replenishment order of `Q` units whenever
    the inventory position is at the reorder point `R` or below.

    If a period is given, the inventory position is checked every `period` time units. Otherwise it is
    checked each time the node's inventory drops.

    Parameters:
        None

    Attributes:
        R (float): Reorder point.
        Q (float): Units in each replenishment order.

    Returns:
        None
    """
    R, Q = self.params['R'], self.params['Q']

    if self.first_review_delay > 0:
        yield self.env.timeout(self.first_review_delay)

    while True:
        self.node.logger.info(f"{self.env.now:.4f}:{self.node.ID}: Inventory levels: {self.node.inventory.level}, on hand: {self.node.inventory.on_hand}")
        if self.node.position() <= R:
            self.node.place_order(Q)

        if self.period == 0:
            yield from self.node.wait_for_drop()
        else:
            yield self.env.timeout(self.period)

PeriodicReplenishment 

PeriodicReplenishment(env, node, params)

Bases: InventoryReplenishment

Implements the periodic replenishment policy: every T time units, the node places a replenishment order of Q units, whatever its inventory position. If a safety stock is given and the inventory level is below it, the order also includes the units needed to bring the inventory level back up to the safety stock. An optional first review delay sets how long to wait before the first order.

The supplier is chosen by the node's supplier-selection policy. If the supplier cannot fill the order at once, a shortage is recorded at the supplier.

def run(self):
    """
    Runs the periodic policy for the whole simulation: places a replenishment order every `T` time units.

    Parameters:
        None

    Attributes:
        T (float): time units between replenishment orders
        Q (float): units in each replenishment order

    Returns:
        None
    """
    T, Q = self.params['T'], self.params['Q']  # the period and the order size
    ss = 0
    if 'safety_stock' in self.params: # check if safety_stock is specified
        validate_non_negative("Safety stock", self.params['safety_stock'])
        self.name = "Periodic with safety replenishment (T, Q, safety_stock)"
        ss = self.params['safety_stock']

    if self.first_review_delay > 0:
        yield self.env.timeout(self.first_review_delay)

    while True:
        self.node.logger.info(f"{self.env.now:.4f}:{self.node.ID}: Inventory levels:{self.node.inventory.level}, on hand:{self.node.inventory.on_hand}")
        reorder_quantity = Q
        if self.node.inventory.level < ss:
            reorder_quantity += ss - self.node.inventory.level
        self.node.place_order(reorder_quantity)
        yield self.env.timeout(T) # wait for the next period

SupplierSelectionPolicy 

SupplierSelectionPolicy(node, mode='fixed', params=None)

Bases: InfoMixin, NamedEntity

The base for all supplier-selection policies: the rules a site follows to choose which of its suppliers receives a replenishment order.

A site reaches each of its suppliers over a link, so the policy works with links: the site's suppliers are the links in node.suppliers, and select returns the link to the chosen supplier (the supplier itself is link.source).

There are two modes: (1) "dynamic": the supplier is chosen afresh for every replenishment order. (2) "fixed": the first supplier chosen is remembered and used for every later order (another one is used only while the remembered supplier or the link to it is disrupted).

Every policy skips a supplier whose site or link is disrupted (see Link.can_take_order). Node.place_order calls select only when at least one supplier can take the order.

Each policy is a subclass that overrides the select method with its own rule.

A site gives its policy the mode and the settings (supplier_selection_param) only when the user gives them, so each policy keeps its own default mode. A policy lists the settings it reads in _param_keys; any other setting is ignored, so a warning names it.

Parameters:
  • node (object) –

    Node for which the supplier selection policy is applied.

  • mode (str, default: 'fixed' ) –

    Supplier selection mode. Must be "dynamic" or "fixed".

  • params (dict, default: None ) –

    Settings for the policy (supplier_selection_param of the site), or None.
Attributes:
  • _info_keys (list) –

    List of keys to include in the info dictionary.

  • _param_keys (tuple) –

    Settings this policy reads from params, or None if it does not say.

  • node (object) –

    Node for which the supplier selection policy is applied.

  • mode (str) –

    Supplier selection mode ("dynamic" or "fixed").

  • params (dict) –

    The settings given to the policy, or None.

  • fixed_supplier (Link) –

    In "fixed" mode, the link to the remembered supplier (None until the first choice).

def __init__(self, node, mode="fixed", params=None):
    """
    Initialize the supplier selection policy object.

    Parameters:
        node (object): Node for which the supplier selection policy is applied.
        mode (str): Supplier selection mode ("dynamic" or "fixed").
        params (dict): Settings for the policy (``supplier_selection_param`` of the site), or None.

    Attributes:
        _info_keys (list): List of keys to include in the info dictionary.
        node (object): Node for which the supplier selection policy is applied.
        mode (str): Supplier selection mode ("dynamic" or "fixed").
        params (dict): The settings given to the policy, or None.
        fixed_supplier (Link): In "fixed" mode, the link to the remembered supplier (None until the first choice).

    Returns:
        None

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the mode is not "dynamic" or "fixed".
        TypeError: If the node is not an instance of Node class.
    """
    if mode not in ["dynamic", "fixed"]:
        global_logger.error(f"Invalid mode: {mode}. Mode must be either 'dynamic' or 'fixed'.")
        raise ValueError("Mode must be either 'dynamic' or 'fixed'.")
    if not isinstance(node, Node):
        global_logger.error("Node must be an instance of Node class.")
        raise TypeError("Node must be an instance of Node class.")
    self.node = node
    self.mode = mode
    self.params = params
    self.fixed_supplier = None
    self._warn_unused_params()

def select(self, order_quantity):
    """
    Chooses the first supplier that can take the order right now.

    Suppliers whose site or link is disrupted are skipped.

    In dynamic mode, the choice is made afresh for each order. In fixed
    mode, the first choice is remembered and used for later orders; while
    it or its link is disrupted, the policy uses another supplier, without
    forgetting the remembered one.

    Returns:

    """

    candidates = self._active_suppliers()
    selected = candidates[0]
    return self._apply_mode(selected)

select(order_quantity)

Chooses the first supplier whose inventory level can fill the whole order.

Suppliers whose site or link is disrupted are skipped first. Among those left, it chooses the first one whose inventory level is at least order_quantity; if none is, it chooses the first of them (the order then waits at that supplier until enough units arrive, and the supplier records a shortage and a backorder).

In fixed mode, the first choice is remembered and used for later orders. While it or its link is disrupted, the policy uses another supplier, without forgetting the remembered one.

  • order_quantity (float) –

    Units in the replenishment order.

    The link to the chosen supplier.

def select(self, order_quantity):
    """
    Chooses the first supplier whose inventory level can fill the whole order.

    Suppliers whose site or link is disrupted are skipped first. Among
    those left, it chooses the first one whose inventory level is at least
    ``order_quantity``; if none is, it chooses the first of them (the order
    then waits at that supplier until enough units arrive, and the supplier
    records a shortage and a backorder).

    In fixed mode, the first choice is remembered and used for later
    orders. While it or its link is disrupted, the policy uses another
    supplier, without forgetting the remembered one.

    Parameters:
        order_quantity (float): Units in the replenishment order.

    Returns:
        Link: The link to the chosen supplier.
    """
    self.validate_suppliers()
    candidates = self._active_suppliers()
    available = [s for s in candidates if s.available_quantity() >= order_quantity]
    selected = available[0] if available else candidates[0]
    return self._apply_mode(selected)

def select(self, order_quantity):

    Suppliers whose site or link is disrupted are skipped first.

def select(self, order_quantity):
    """
    Chooses the supplier with the shortest lead time.

    Suppliers whose site or link is disrupted are skipped first.

    In fixed mode, the first choice is remembered and used for later
    orders. While it or its link is disrupted, the policy uses another
    supplier, without forgetting the remembered one.

    Parameters:
        order_quantity (float): Units in the replenishment order.

    Returns:
        Link: The link to the chosen supplier.
    """
    self.validate_suppliers()
    candidates = self._active_suppliers()
    selected = min(candidates, key=lambda s: s.lead_time())
    return self._apply_mode(selected)

SelectProbabilistic 

SelectProbabilistic(node, mode='dynamic', params=None)

Bases: SupplierSelectionPolicy

Chooses the supplier of each replenishment order at random, with a probability for each supplier.

For example, a retailer that sends half of its orders to distributor D1, 30% to D2 and 20% to D3 is given supplier_selection_param={"probabilities": {"D1": 0.5, "D2": 0.3, "D3": 0.2}}. The probabilities are keyed by supplier ID (link.source.ID), so they can be given before the links exist, and they must sum to 1. A supplier with probability 0 is never chosen.

For every order the policy draws exactly one random number u between 0 and 1 and puts the probabilities side by side, in the order the links to the suppliers were created: with 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2, u below 0.5 chooses the first supplier, u from 0.5 to below 0.8 the second, and the rest the third. One number per order means that two runs with the same seed see the same numbers, so changing a probability a little changes only the few orders whose number falls near a boundary.

The probabilities are the shares of the orders while every supplier can take orders. When a supplier or the link to it is disrupted, on_disruption decides what happens:

  • "rescale" (the default): the order goes to one of the other suppliers, which keep their ratios. With 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 and the first supplier disrupted, the other two get 0.6 and 0.4.
  • "block": the draw uses the given probabilities as they are. If it chooses a disrupted supplier, the order is not placed and is counted as blocked; the site orders again when a supplier or a link recovers, or when its inventory drops.

So with disruptions, the shares of the orders at the end of a run differ from the probabilities. The link statistics (link.stats) record the real shares. The stored probabilities never change.

The mode is always "dynamic" (a new choice for every order); "fixed" would keep the first random choice for ever, so it is rejected.

Parameters:
  • node (object) –

    The site that uses the policy.

  • mode (str, default: 'dynamic' ) –

    "dynamic" (the default and the only mode allowed).

  • params (dict, default: None ) –

    The settings, all optional: probabilities (dict from supplier ID to probability; may also be given later with set_probabilities), on_disruption ("rescale" or "block"), and seed (a number or a string) or rng (a random.Random) for the policy's own random numbers. With neither, a seed is drawn once from the site's random number generator (node.rng), so scm.set_seed still makes runs repeatable.

def __init__(self, node, mode="dynamic", params=None):
    """
    Initialize the policy.

    Parameters:
        node (object): The site that uses the policy.
        mode (str): "dynamic" (the default and the only mode allowed).
        params (dict): The settings (see the class description), or None.

    Returns:
        None

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the mode is "fixed", a setting has a wrong value, or both ``seed`` and ``rng`` are given.
    """
    if mode == "fixed":
        message = (f"{getattr(node, 'ID', '?')}: SelectProbabilistic makes a new random choice for every order, "
                   f"so it cannot be used in 'fixed' mode. Leave supplier_selection_mode out, or use 'dynamic'.")
        global_logger.error(message)
        raise ValueError(message)
    super().__init__(node, mode, params)
    self.name = "Probability-based supplier"
    params = params if params is not None else {}
    if not isinstance(params, dict):
        global_logger.error(f"{node.ID}: supplier_selection_param must be a dict.")
        raise ValueError("supplier_selection_param must be a dict.")

    self.on_disruption = params.get("on_disruption", "rescale")
    if self.on_disruption not in ("rescale", "block"):
        message = f"{node.ID}: on_disruption must be 'rescale' or 'block', not {self.on_disruption!r}."
        global_logger.error(message)
        raise ValueError(message)

    # The policy's own random numbers, so its draws never shift any other
    # random numbers in the simulation (for example those of disruptions).
    # A seed or rng of None counts as not given, so a script that passes
    # seed=config.get("seed") without a seed still repeats with scm.set_seed.
    seed, rng = params.get("seed"), params.get("rng")
    if seed is not None and rng is not None:
        message = f"{node.ID}: give either seed or rng to SelectProbabilistic, not both."
        global_logger.error(message)
        raise ValueError(message)
    if rng is not None:
        if not isinstance(rng, random.Random):
            message = f"{node.ID}: rng must be a random.Random object."
            global_logger.error(message)
            raise ValueError(message)
        self.rng = rng
    elif seed is not None:
        if isinstance(seed, numbers.Integral):
            seed = int(seed)  # a numpy integer, for example, becomes a Python int
        if not isinstance(seed, (int, float, str, bytes, bytearray)):
            message = f"{node.ID}: seed must be a number or a string, not {seed!r}."
            global_logger.error(message)
            raise ValueError(message)
        self.rng = random.Random(seed)
    else:
        # One number from the site's generator (the library's, unless the
        # site has its own), so scm.set_seed still makes the run repeatable.
        self.rng = random.Random(self.node.rng.getrandbits(64))

    self.probabilities = None
    self._links_checked = False
    if params.get("probabilities") is not None:
        self.set_probabilities(params["probabilities"])

def set_probabilities(self, probabilities):
    """
    Set or replace the probabilities of the suppliers.

    The links are checked against them at the next order (not at once,
    because more links may still be added).

    Parameters:
        probabilities (dict): The probability of each supplier, by supplier ID. None may be negative, at
            least one must be above 0, and together they must sum to 1.

    Returns:
        None

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the probabilities are not a dict of numbers that sum to 1, or one is negative.
    """
    def fail(reason):
        message = f"{self.node.ID}: the probabilities of SelectProbabilistic {reason}."
        global_logger.error(message)
        raise ValueError(message)

    if not isinstance(probabilities, dict):
        fail("must be a dict from supplier ID to probability")
    for supplier_id, p in probabilities.items():
        if isinstance(p, bool) or not isinstance(p, numbers.Real) or not math.isfinite(p):
            fail(f"must be numbers ({supplier_id!r} has {p!r})")
        if p < 0:
            fail(f"cannot be negative ({supplier_id!r} has {p})")
    total = sum(probabilities.values())
    if not any(p > 0 for p in probabilities.values()):
        fail("must have at least one above 0")
    if abs(total - 1) > 1e-6:  # a little room for rounding, as in 0.1 + 0.2 + 0.7
        fail(f"must sum to 1, not {total}")
    self.probabilities = dict(probabilities)  # a copy, so later changes to the user's dict have no effect
    self._links_checked = False

Check the probabilities against the links to the site's suppliers: the probabilities have been given, every link has a probability, every probability has a link, and no supplier has two links to this site (its ID would not say which link is meant). A link or ID left over is most likely a typo, so it is an error, not a probability of 0. create_sc_net calls this once every link is created, and select calls it before its first choice.

def check_links(self):
    """
    Check the probabilities against the links to the site's suppliers: the probabilities have been given,
    every link has a probability, every probability has a link, and no supplier has two links to this site
    (its ID would not say which link is meant). A link or ID left over is most likely a typo, so it is an
    error, not a probability of 0. ``create_sc_net`` calls this once every link is created, and ``select``
    calls it before its first choice.

    Returns:
        None

    Raises:
        ValueError: If any of these checks fails.
    """
    def fail(reason):
        message = f"{self.node.ID}: SelectProbabilistic {reason}."
        global_logger.error(message)
        raise ValueError(message)

    if self.probabilities is None:
        fail("has no probabilities. Give them in supplier_selection_param or with set_probabilities")
    linked = [link.source.ID for link in self.node.suppliers]
    twice = sorted({str(i) for i in linked if linked.count(i) > 1})
    if twice:
        fail(f"cannot tell apart two links from the same supplier ({', '.join(twice)})")
    missing = [str(i) for i in linked if i not in self.probabilities]
    if missing:
        fail(f"has no probability for the supplier(s) {', '.join(missing)}, linked to this site")
    unlinked = sorted(str(i) for i in self.probabilities if i not in linked)
    if unlinked:
        fail(f"has a probability for the supplier(s) {', '.join(unlinked)}, which have no link to this site")
    self._links_checked = True

Chooses the supplier of one replenishment order at random.

With "rescale", the choice is made among the suppliers that can take the order (if none with a probability above 0 can, the chosen supplier is disrupted and the order is blocked). With "block", the choice is made among all suppliers with a probability above 0. A disrupted supplier returned here is blocked by InventoryNode.process_order, which counts the order as blocked.

def select(self, order_quantity):
    """
    Chooses the supplier of one replenishment order at random.

    With ``"rescale"``, the choice is made among the suppliers that can take the order (if none with a
    probability above 0 can, the chosen supplier is disrupted and the order is blocked). With ``"block"``,
    the choice is made among all suppliers with a probability above 0. A disrupted supplier returned here
    is blocked by ``InventoryNode.process_order``, which counts the order as ``blocked``.

    Parameters:
        order_quantity (float): Units in the replenishment order.

    Returns:
        Link: The link to the chosen supplier.
    """
    if not self._links_checked:
        self.check_links()
    u = self.rng.random()  # exactly one number for every order
    candidates = [(link, self.probabilities[link.source.ID]) for link in self.node.suppliers
                  if self.probabilities[link.source.ID] > 0]
    choices = candidates  # the suppliers this order can go to
    if self.on_disruption == "rescale":
        working = [(link, p) for link, p in candidates if link.can_take_order()]
        if working:
            choices = working
    # Scaling u by the total probability of these suppliers shares out the
    # probability of the suppliers left out, keeping their ratios.
    target = u * sum(p for _, p in choices)
    running = 0.0
    for link, p in choices:
        running += p
        if target < running:
            return link
    return choices[-1][0]  # rounding left u just past the end

Node 

Node(env: Environment, ID: str, name: str, node_type: str, failure_p: float = 0.0, node_disrupt_time: Callable = None, node_recovery_time: Callable = lambda: 1, logging: bool = True, rng: Random = None, disruption_impact=None, disruption_loss_fraction=1.0, **kwargs)

Bases: NamedEntity, InfoMixin

Represents a node in the supply chain network: a raw-material supplier, a manufacturer, a warehouse, distributor or retailer, or a customer demand. This is the base class they all share. It handles disruption and recovery, and logging.

A node can be disrupted at random (each time unit, a disruption starts with probability failure_p) or at the times given by node_disrupt_time. While disrupted, its status is "inactive"; it recovers after node_recovery_time. The subclasses also keep statistics (stats): orders, shortages, costs, revenue and profit.

Sites can use the built-in replenishment policies ((s, S), (R, Q) and periodic) or a custom one made by subclassing InventoryReplenishment, and the built-in supplier-selection policies (SelectFirst, SelectAvailable, SelectCheapest, SelectFastest) or a custom one made by subclassing SupplierSelectionPolicy.

For the node types, see NodeType.

Parameters:
  • env (Environment) –

    Simulation environment.

  • ID (str) –

    Unique node ID.

  • name (str) –

    Node name.

  • node_type (str) –

    Type of the node.

  • failure_p (float, default: 0.0 ) –

    Disruption probability: the chance, each time unit, that a disruption starts.

  • node_disrupt_time (callable, default: None ) –

    Time units until the next disruption (a number, or a function returning one each time).

  • node_recovery_time (callable, default: lambda: 1 ) –

    Time units a disruption lasts (a number, or a function returning one each time).

  • logging (bool, default: True ) –

    Flag to enable/disable logging.

  • disruption_impact (str | callable | None, default: None ) –

    What a disruption does to the units at the node, at the moment it starts. None (default) leaves them untouched. Built-in names: "destroy_all" destroys all units at the node (and a manufacturer's raw materials); "destroy_fraction" destroys disruption_loss_fraction × inventory level. For any other effect (partial spoilage, contamination, capacity damage), pass your own function f(node) -> None. It runs once per disruption; for an effect that builds up during the disruption, start a SimPy process inside the function.

  • disruption_loss_fraction (float | callable, default: 1.0 ) –

    Fraction between 0 and 1, used with disruption_impact="destroy_fraction". May be a zero-arg function, so each disruption can destroy a different fraction.

  • **kwargs –

    Additional arguments for the logger.

def __init__(self, env: simpy.Environment,
             ID: str,
             name: str,
             node_type: str,
             failure_p:float = 0.0,
             node_disrupt_time: Callable = None,
             node_recovery_time: Callable = lambda: 1,
             logging: bool = True,
             rng: random.Random = None,
             disruption_impact=None,
             disruption_loss_fraction=1.0,
             **kwargs) -> None:
    """
    Initialize the node object.

    Parameters:
        env (simpy.Environment): Simulation environment.
        ID (str): Unique node ID.
        name (str): Node name.
        node_type (str): Type of the node.
        failure_p (float, optional): Disruption probability: the chance, each time unit, that a disruption starts.
        node_disrupt_time (callable, optional): Time units until the next disruption (a number or a function).
        node_recovery_time (callable, optional): Time units a disruption lasts (a number or a function).
        logging (bool, optional): Flag to enable/disable logging.
        **kwargs: Additional arguments for the logger.

    Attributes:
        _info_keys (list): List of keys to include in the info dictionary.  
        env (simpy.Environment): simulation environment
        ID (str): ID of the node (alphanumeric)
        name (str): name of the node
        node_type (str): type of the node
        node_failure_p (float): disruption probability
        node_status (str): status of the node: "active", or "inactive" while disrupted
        node_disrupt_time (callable): function giving the time units until the next disruption
        node_recovery_time (callable): function giving the time units a disruption lasts
        logger (GlobalLogger): logger object

    Returns:
        None
    """
    if not isinstance(env, simpy.Environment):
        raise ValueError("Invalid environment. Provide a valid SimPy environment.")
    # Validate node_type via the NodeType enum — single source of truth
    # shared with create_sc_net. Accepts either a string (case-insensitive)
    # or a NodeType member. Stored as the normalized lowercase string so
    # every existing equality check against a literal (``== "demand"``,
    # ``"supplier" in node.node_type``) continues to work.
    try:
        node_type = NodeType(node_type).value
    except ValueError:
        global_logger.error(f"Invalid node type. Node type: {node_type}")
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid node type: {node_type}.")
    # ``ensure_numeric_callable`` turns a plain number into a function that
    # returns it, and calls the function once to check that it returns a
    # number. A mistake (for example, passing a class such as ``int``) is
    # then reported here, instead of crashing later in the middle of a run.
    node_recovery_time = ensure_numeric_callable("node_recovery_time", node_recovery_time)
    if node_disrupt_time is not None:
        node_disrupt_time = ensure_numeric_callable("node_disrupt_time", node_disrupt_time)
    self.env = env  # simulation environment
    self.ID = ID  # ID of the node (alphanumeric)
    self.name = name  # name of the node
    self.node_type = node_type  # type of the node (see NodeType)
    self.node_failure_p = failure_p  # disruption probability
    self.node_status = "active"  # "active", or "inactive" while disrupted
    self.node_disrupt_time = node_disrupt_time  # function: time units until the next disruption
    self.node_recovery_time = node_recovery_time  # function: time units a disruption lasts
    self.rng = rng if rng is not None else _rng  # random number generator for random disruptions; the library's default if none is given
    self.suppliers = []  # links to this node's suppliers; filled in by Link.__init__ through add_supplier_link
    self.buyers = []  # links to this node's buyers; filled in by Link.__init__ through add_buyer_link
    # Work out the disruption-impact function once, here. The setting as
    # given is kept as ``disruption_impact`` (shown by get_info); the
    # function that runs when a disruption starts is ``_disruption_impact_fn``.
    self.disruption_impact = disruption_impact
    self._disruption_impact_fn = _resolve_disruption_impact(disruption_impact, disruption_loss_fraction)

    logger_name = self.ID # default logger name is the node ID
    if 'logger_name' in kwargs:
        logger_name = kwargs.pop('logger_name')
    # Per-node loggers live as children of the library root ``"sim_trace"``
    # so their records propagate up to the single set of handlers configured
    # on ``global_logger``. This avoids each Node opening its own
    # FileHandler on ``simulation_trace.log`` (which used to truncate the
    # file once per node at construction). Users who pass a custom
    # ``logger_name`` get the prefix added automatically; if they already
    # supplied the prefix we don't double it.
    if not logger_name.startswith("sim_trace."):
        logger_name = f"sim_trace.{logger_name}"
    # Only forward kwargs that GlobalLogger actually accepts; ignore the rest
    # so unrelated keys (e.g. record_inv_levels, shelf_life) don't raise TypeError.
    logger_kwargs = {k: kwargs[k] for k in kwargs if k in _LOGGER_KWARGS}
    self.logger = GlobalLogger(logger_name=logger_name, **logger_kwargs)  # create a logger
    # Do NOT call enable_logging() here — the per-node logger inherits its
    # handlers from ``global_logger`` via propagation. The historical call
    # site re-attached a FileHandler in mode='w' on every Node, which
    # truncated the trace file N times during network construction (§4.8).
    if not logging:
        self.logger.disable_logging()  # mute this node specifically

    if(self.node_failure_p>0 or self.node_disrupt_time): # start the disruption process if the node can be disrupted
        self.env.process(self.disruption())
